chunks: Al-Tawhid: Al-Attar, from Sa'd, from Ibn Yazid, from al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Khazzaz, from Muthanna al-Hannat, from Abu Ja'far - I think he is Muhammad ibn al-Nu'man - who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic:
And He is Allah in the heavens and in the earth.

He said: Thus He is in every place. I said: By His essence? He said: Woe be upon you! Physical spaces have limits, so if you were to say 'in a place by His essence' it would be necessary for you to say 'in limits and other such (deficiencies)'. Rather, He is distinct from His creation, encompassing what He created in terms of knowledge, power, awareness, and authority. His knowledge of what is in the earth is not less than that in the heaven. Nothing becomes distant from Him, and all things are equal to Him in terms of knowledge, power, authority, ownership, and awareness.
ai.seo_question: How does Shia theology interpret God being 'in the heavens and in the earth' without being physically located there?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the verse 'He is in the heavens and in the earth' by distinguishing between God's essence and spatial dimensions, asserting that He is distinct from His creation yet encompassing it through knowledge and power. It refutes the idea of divine confinement to specific locations, emphasizing that God's attributes are uniform across all realms, whether in the heavens or the earth. This aligns with Shia theological principles of divine transcendence (tanzih) while affirming His immanence through omnipresence of knowledge and power.
